seo.title: Karmic tail 3 16 4 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 16 4 compatibility: why a couple's Empress and Emperor have the Tower between them, not the Chariot, and what the tale of Aladdin knows.

title: The couple's karmic tail 3-16-4: from the Empress to the Emperor through the Tower
short: The couple's tail 3-16-4 opens with the Empress and closes with the Emperor — the queen and king of the major arcana, whom an old tradition, Waite notes, takes for husband and wife. Between them stands the Tower, struck by lightning. The riddle is that by the ordinary arithmetic of the matrix the Chariot should have stood there. The answer is written in the numbers themselves: the couple enters the task wanting a home with plenty of everything, passes through the collapse of what rested on one partner's knowledge and the other's ignorance, and learns the main thing — to hold power and order together, not in one person's pocket.

sections.h2: How the 3-16-4 tail is formed: a worked example
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is above 22, its digits are added. The middle of the couple's tail is also built from the partners' middles, not worked out from the two outer numbers.

The example uses two dates, 07.01.1976 (7 January 1976) and 11.02.1976 (11 February 1976). The first person has the personal tail 21-7-13 (The World, The Chariot, Death) and centre 8. The second has 9-9-18 (The Hermit, The Hermit, The Moon) and centre 9.

This meeting is the only road to the tail. In 100% of couples with the tail 3-16-4, one partner has the personal tail 21-7-13 and the other 9-9-18. Neither personal tail is common: 21-7-13 belongs to roughly one person in 68, 9-9-18 to one in 50. Hence the couple's rarity: one couple in 1,712 (0.058%), 89th place among the 97 couple tails.

As a personal tail, 3-16-4 does not occur for any date. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. This is a tail that exists only for two.
The couple in the example has 6, The Lovers, in its values. More on them, and on the Star in the centre, below.

sections.h2: The first clue: the Chariot could have stood where the Tower is
paragraphs: Add the outer numbers of the tail the way a personal matrix does: 3 + 4 = 7, the seventh arcanum, The Chariot. Between the Empress and the Emperor the arithmetic of the matrix leaves exactly two options. In every personal tail the middle is the reduced sum of the entry and the task, and reduction never changes the remainder after division by nine. So the couple's middle leaves the same remainder as 3 + 4: it can only be 7 or 16. The tail 3-7-4, with the Chariot, occurs in one couple in 217. The tail 3-16-4, with the Tower, in one in 1,712 — eight times rarer.

And the Chariot is here. It stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail, 21-7-13. The other partner simply brings a Hermit to the same point, and 7 + 9 make 16. **This couple's Tower is built from a chariot that drives off and a lantern that stays at home.**

Waite's divinatory lists hint at what the two halves are made of. His Chariot is "Succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption", and its conquests, Waite writes, are "manifest or external and not within himself". The Hermit reversed is "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution." One rides out after victories. The other guards something and keeps quiet. Taken apart, these are just two different temperaments, and neither is dangerous on its own. Added together at one point of the couple's matrix, they make lightning.

This is no verdict on anyone's character: that is how the numbers add up, and in real life both partners get to play both parts. How exactly a chariot and a lantern bring a house down is shown best not by the tarot but by a fairy tale.

sections.h2: The tale this couple lives in
paragraphs: "Aladdin" has no Arabic original. On 5 May 1709 the orientalist Antoine Galland wrote in his Paris diary: "In the morning, the Maronite Hanna of Aleppo finished telling me the tale of the Lamp." Hanna Diyab, a young traveller who had come to France with the antiquities collector Paul Lucas, told Galland more than a dozen stories. "The Story of Aladdin, or the Wonderful Lamp" came out in the ninth and tenth volumes of Galland's "Thousand and One Nights" in the early 1710s. The Arabic manuscripts of the tale found later turned out to be back-translations from the French, as the Nights scholar Muhsin Mahdi showed. That is why every quotation below follows Galland, in our own translation from the French.

In the children's version this is a story about a boy and a genie. In Galland it is a story about a marriage, and it runs in the order of the tail's three cards. First, a palace that grows overnight opposite the sultan's palace: the Empress. Then a lamp given away as a joke while the master is out hunting, and the palace vanishing overnight with the wife inside: the Tower. At the end, two people on one throne: the Emperor. Between the second and third acts there is one more scene, without which the tale would be about magic rather than about a couple — a conversation in Africa about whose fault it was.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Empress: a palace with one unfinished window
paragraphs: The entry point is what the couple wants together, its shared wishes and agreements. In the relationship section of the reading the same point is labelled "Common language". For a 3-16-4 couple the common language is abundance. A home they want furnished at once. Gifts that speak instead of words. Plans in which everything is big: a flat, children, travel, a business of their own. The urge to build is shared from the first day, and it easily turns into action.

Galland gives this wish an exact shape. Aladdin puts off the wedding: first there must be a palace "worthy to receive the princess". The genie builds it overnight — porphyry, jasper, agate, and at the top a domed hall with twenty-four windows set with diamonds, rubies and emeralds; a garden, kitchens, storerooms, stables and, as a separate line of the order, "not forgetting a hunting train". The Chariot is built into the house from day one.

One window Aladdin orders to be left unfinished. The sultan, his future father-in-law, is puzzled: was it forgotten? was there no time? Aladdin replies that it was done on purpose, so that His Majesty might have the glory of completing the hall. The sultan's jewellers spend a month and the treasury's stones and do not finish even half. Galland says it plainly: Aladdin "concealed the real reason" — the sultan simply did not have enough jewels. The window was a polite trap, a place left to the in-laws so that they could see for themselves that this house was beyond them.

The same entry also shows the downside of the Empress that Lisovskaya writes about: the task of getting out from under the family's influence. The palace stands "opposite the sultan's palace, at a proper distance", and the genie lays a velvet carpet from the father-in-law's door to the princess's rooms. Every morning, as was his habit, the sultan steps up to an open window to admire the young couple's palace. The couple lives in full view of the family, on the family's carpet, with the family's window in its own hall. That kind of task does not begin with a quarrel; it begins with a carpet.

Waite seems to describe both faces of this entry in a single line. His Empress is "Fruitfulness, action, initiative" and, straight after, "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance". A palace and ignorance in one card. A few years later, ignorance will become the key detail of the tale.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Tower: "Who will exchange old lamps for new?"
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail is how the couple lives the road from the shared wish to the main task. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own — it only adds to the main task; we read it as the road. For 3-16-4 the road runs through the Tower.

Galland stages the scene with a watchmaker's precision. Aladdin goes hunting for eight days — he goes hunting every week. The lamp without which he would have neither palace nor wife he puts on the cornice of the hall of twenty-four windows himself, "for fear of losing it". The rest of the time he carries it on him. In his absences neither the maids nor the eunuchs nor the princess herself had ever paid it any attention.

A few days later a madman with a basket of shiny new copper lamps appears under the windows, crying: "Who will exchange old lamps for new?" The children jeer, a maid comes back into the hall choking with laughter, and the princess, watching her, laughs too. Another maid remembers the old lamp on the cornice: the master will hardly mind finding a new one in its place. The princess, Galland writes, did not know how precious the lamp was, and she "went along with the joke". At night the magician rubs the lamp, and the palace, with the princess in it, is carried off to Africa.

Here Galland does something rare for a fairy tale: he stops and speaks to the reader. "It will be said that Aladdin's precaution was a good one, but that he should at least have locked the lamp away. That is true; but such mistakes have been made in every age, they are made still, and they will never stop being made." No better caption could be written for this couple's Tower.

In the morning the sultan, as usual, goes to the window to admire the palace and sees an empty space, "just as it was before anything was built there". He rubs his eyes and reasons: had the palace collapsed, there would be heaps of stone; had the earth swallowed it, there would be some trace. There is neither. Waite's Tower is "Misery… deception, ruin", "in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". **This couple's Tower is often exactly that: from outside nothing is broken, and yet the old home is gone.**

The mechanism is now in full view. Neither of the two caused the collapse. One held the house's support in hand and, leaving, put it where it could not be seen — out of caution, not cunning. The other did not know it was a support and, in a good-faith joke, swapped the old for the new. The chariot drove off, the lantern stayed unexplained, and together they made the Tower. Among the Tower's tasks Lisovskaya also lists partners who, in trouble, look in different directions. The tale shows this literally: the sultan demands Aladdin's head, while in Africa the magician tells the princess her husband has been executed. Each is left with half of the truth.

sections.h2: After the lightning: taking the blame on yourself
paragraphs: Lisovskaya's key to the Tower in a couple is that an ordeal survived together makes the union stronger. Galland shows where "together" begins. Aladdin finds the princess in Africa, and the first thing he asks is where the old lamp from the cornice went. What follows is a dialogue that children's versions cut down to a single line.
The princess: "I did suspect that our shared misfortune came from that lamp, and what torments me most is that I am the cause of it myself!"
Aladdin: "Do not take the blame; it is all mine — I should have kept it more carefully. Let us think only of how to repair this loss."

These two lines turn the Tower towards the Emperor. Each takes the blame, and so there is no longer any need to look for a culprit. The one who held the lamp admits that it was his to guard. And straight away there is a plan with roles: Aladdin promises to be back by noon and explain what the princess must do for it to succeed.

The plan rests on a second exchange. The princess puts on her finest dress, receives the magician kindly and at supper offers to swap cups: "with us in China", she says, lovers hand each other their cups and drink to one another. Her cup holds Aladdin's powder, and the fairy-tale villain gets what he deserves. **The first exchange she made without knowing what it meant, and the palace vanished. The second she made understanding it better than anyone at the table, and the palace came back.** Later she will tell her father about the measures they took "jointly". The difference between the Tower and its repair fits into that one word.

sections.h2: The roc's egg: when a shared wish becomes resistance
paragraphs: The entry point stands on the line of tasks, and so it has a second face: the wish that leads the couple can become its resistance. Galland shows this in an episode that cartoons usually leave out.

The magician had a younger brother. He kills the holy woman Fatima, a recluse who left her cell only on Mondays and Fridays, puts on her dress and veil, and the princess, who has long wanted to meet the saint, herself gives her rooms in the palace. Aladdin is out hunting again, for the sixth day. The false Fatima looks round the hall and says humbly: "As far as a recluse who knows nothing of what the world calls beautiful can judge, one thing is missing here." A roc's egg hanging from the dome.

Aladdin comes home to find his wife a little cool. "I believed, as you did, that our palace was the most magnificent and perfect in the world," she says, and now the palace lacks an egg. Aladdin answers with a sentence that holds the Empress's whole common language: "It is enough that you find a roc's egg missing here for me to find the same flaw." He rubs the lamp, and the genie lets out a cry that shakes the hall: "Is it not enough that my companions and I have done everything for you — and now you demand that I bring you my master and hang him in the middle of this dome?" The wish, the genie explains, came not from them but from an enemy in disguise.

This is a precise drawing of how a 3-16-4 couple's entry turns into resistance. Danger arrives not as an enemy but as modest advice from under someone else's veil: "everyone has one already", "the home only lacks…", "you have to, for the children". A couple whose common language is abundance picks the wish up at once: if you want it, then so do I. The genie hears sacrilege in the request: to hang under the dome his own master, the power he himself serves. In the same way the last thing "for perfect completeness" can demand that a couple hang under the dome the very source of everything else: strength, money, the freedom of one of the two. Waite describes the Hermit reversed with the words "Concealment, disguise", and in the tale trouble comes a second time from a false hermit — again while the master is out hunting.

sections.h2: Main task — The Emperor: "They reigned together"
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is the couple's main task, and it is read mostly through its downside: what does not work and what has to be learned. Here it is the Emperor: power, structure, rules, responsibility. Waite's Emperor is "Stability, power, protection, realization… also authority and will". Waite himself stresses that this card and the Empress "do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied", and in his historical survey he calls the Emperor "by imputation the spouse of the former". The tail 3-16-4 is the road from a queen to her husband, and it leads through the Tower.

Here is Galland's ending. A few years later the sultan dies at a great age. He has no sons, and the princess, "as lawful heir", succeeds him and shares the supreme power with Aladdin. "They reigned together for many years."

In Andrew Lang's "Blue Fairy Book" (1889), one of the best-known English retellings, the ending is shorter: "He succeeded the Sultan when he died, and reigned for many years." The heiress and the word "together" are gone. **The reteller did to the end of the tale what the Emperor at his worst does to a couple: one crown, one head.**

Wen offers a guess about the models for these two cards, and calls it speculation herself: the Empress as Joan I of Navarre, the Emperor as her husband Philip IV of France. The guess has the same shape as Galland's ending. Joan became Queen of Navarre in her own right before she was two; Philip ruled Navarre together with her. The kingdom comes through one, and two rule it.

What does this Emperor demand of a 3-16-4 couple? The downside of the Emperor that Lisovskaya describes shows up in such a couple as scenes. One partner runs the budget and announces decisions already made. A rule invented in a hard year gets in both partners' way five years later, yet dropping it feels like admitting weakness. "Are you upset?" is met with "I'm fine", and the argument about who is in charge replaces the conversation about what hurt. The tale adds one subtle point to the list. After Africa, Aladdin always carries the lamp on him, wherever he goes: the lesson has been learned as control, not as shared knowledge. And the next trouble comes through another door — through his wife's wish and a stranger's veil. One hand on the lamp does not save the house if the other partner does not know what holds it up.

The last clue comes from Scheherazade herself. Having finished the tale, she explains to her sultan husband what it teaches: a good and just monarch risks even losing his throne when "through unreasonable haste he condemns an innocent man without being willing to hear his defence". She means the father-in-law, who nearly beheaded Aladdin on the first morning after the palace disappeared. For a 3-16-4 couple this is the Emperor at his best: listen first, decide afterwards.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: what Waite saw in the Hermit's lantern
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In every 3-16-4 couple the Star stands there, 17. No person ever has 17 in the centre: this card appears in the centre only for a couple. It is built from the partners' personal centres — Justice (8) for the owner of the tail 21-7-13 and the Hermit (9) for the owner of 9-9-18.

In the deck the Star comes straight after the Tower: the sixteenth card is the lightning, the seventeenth is the light that follows it. This couple's atmosphere is the card that arrives after the collapse.

And in his description of the Hermit, Waite left a sentence that links the middle of the tail to the couple's centre: "It is a star which shines in the lantern." The Hermit is the very card whose nine turned the Chariot into the Tower. His lantern is both the lamp on the cornice and the star in the centre. **The same knowledge, hidden with one partner, brings the palace down; shared between two, it becomes the light the couple lives in.**

Waite's divinatory list for the Star is split in two: "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment; another reading says—hope and bright prospects". The tale of Aladdin fits into that line: the theft of the lamp, the lost palace, the princess abandoned in Africa — and the hope with which Aladdin wakes under her window to birdsong.

Lisovskaya describes the Star in a couple's atmosphere in a way that echoes the whole task of the tail. At its best the union inspires both, and this is the rare case when the pretty picture really is the truth. At its worst come things left unsaid and an infatuation that takes no responsibility. The Star feels at home in a beautiful palace. The Emperor demands that the palace have a foundation both of them know about.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are one more answer to the question of what the two are together for. In 3-16-4 couples one of two cards stands there.

**The Lovers, 6 — in 75.5% of such couples.** Waite gives them the list "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome" and recalls an old title of the card, Simulacrum fidei, "the symbol of conjugal faith". This is the value of choice: the union holds because the two choose each other again, including after the Tower. In Africa the princess chooses Aladdin while the magician tells her every day that her husband is dead.

**The Devil, 15 — in 24.5%.** In Waite this card is "the chain and fatality of the material life". In the tale it has an exact double: the genie, who calls himself the slave "of all who have the lamp in hand". He serves Aladdin, he serves the magician — whoever holds the lamp. The strength of such a couple is that what they share holds them firmly: the home, the business, what they have built. The risk is that the couple starts serving its palace, while the palace serves whoever holds the lamp. Here the Emperor's task is sharpest of all: power in the home must not go to whoever grabs the lamp first.

sections.h2: How to recognise yourselves in this tale
paragraphs: The tale is not a prediction. The Tower in the tail does not promise that the home will vanish, nor the Emperor that someone will become a tyrant. It is the outline of a task, and it is usually recognised by small things.

ul: **The lamp on the cornice.** One of the two knows what holds the home up: where the documents and passwords are, how the payments and debts work, what was agreed with the landlord or the family, where the money in the shared business really comes from. They are not hiding it — it is just "safer this way" and "why burden you with it".
**The hunt.** The same person is often away: a project, business trips, a season, a big goal. The Chariot rides out after victories, and that is temperament, not a vice.

**The exchange in jest.** The other, not knowing that the "old" thing holds the home up, swaps it for something new in good faith: throws out papers that look useless, accepts a relative's generous offer, closes a "spare" account. It is all done lightly, sometimes with a laugh.
**The velvet carpet.** The family lives close by and admires the home from its own window; inside the home there is a place left to them "for the glory", and advice comes in through that place.
**The roc's egg.** The home always lacks one more thing, and one partner's wish instantly becomes both partners' wish.
**The empty space.** When the collapse comes, it looks less like a row than like a disappearance: nothing is smashed, and yet the old life is gone.

paragraphs: The roles are not fixed and have nothing to do with gender. Whoever holds the lamp today may swap someone else's lamp for a new one tomorrow. Recognising oneself in both roles is already half the task.

sections.h2: What changes the script: an inventory of lamps
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail 3-16-4 is Galland's ending: the same palace, ruled by two. In Lisovskaya the Emperor at his best is a couple whose rules suit both, where each has an area of responsibility and strictness never turns into fanaticism. For a 3-16-4 couple it is made of a few habits.

ul: **An inventory of lamps.** Every so often, list together what holds the home up: money, documents, access, obligations, agreements with the family. The point is not inspection but making sure no lamp stands on a cornice that only one partner knows about.
**Leaving? Leave a map.** Before the "hunt", say where things are and what must not be changed without a call. One sentence would have been enough for Aladdin.
**Rules for two — with a review date.** The Emperor at his worst makes rules that later get in the way. A rule the couple wrote itself, it can also rewrite.
**After a collapse, the formula from Africa.** Do not look for a culprit; take your share of the blame and go straight to the plan: "let us think only of how to repair".
**The roc's egg test.** Before adding the last thing "for perfect completeness", ask whose wish it is and who suggested it.
**Listen first, decide afterwards.** Scheherazade's rule for a monarch works in any kitchen where decisions are made for two.

paragraphs: If threats, pressure or fear for each other appear in the home, this is no longer a tale about a lamp or a task of the tail. Then a psychologist is needed, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.

ul: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** What the couple wants together: a home, prosperity, growth, everything big and everything at once. This is their common language, and it turns into resistance when the wishes outgrow the foundations.
**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** How the couple travels the road: through a sudden collapse. What falls is whatever rested on a secret that one kept out of caution and the other never knew.
**Main task — 4, The Emperor.** What the couple has to learn: shared order, rules and power agreed by both; responsibility without despotism and without hunting for someone to blame.

intro: This couple's plot was written down long ago, and everyone knows it. Aladdin's palace rose in a single night and vanished in a single night, while its master was out hunting and his wife, laughing, handed a street trader an old lamp from the cornice, not knowing that the whole palace rested on it. What follows is an investigation: clues in the numbers, in Waite and Wen, and in the first, French text of the tale, whose ending is not the one in the children's version.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3-16-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple who enter the relationship with a shared wish for a home and abundance (The Empress, 3), pass through a sudden collapse of what rested on one partner's knowledge and the other's ignorance (The Tower, 16), and learn to build shared order and share power (The Emperor, 4). The tail exists only for couples, roughly one in 1,712.

faq.q: Why is the Tower in the middle and not the Chariot, if 3 + 4 = 7?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not worked out from the outer numbers: it is built from the middles of the partners' personal tails. For every 3-16-4 couple this is 7 + 9 = 16 — one partner's Chariot and the other's Hermit. By the rules of reduction, only 7 or 16 can stand between 3 and 4; the variant with the Chariot, 3-7-4, occurs eight times more often.

faq.q: Does the tail 3-16-4 occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail is the sum of the main task and the centre, and with a main task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. 3-16-4 is a tail of the couple's matrix only, and in every such couple it is built from the personal tails 21-7-13 and 9-9-18.

faq.q: Does the Tower mean the couple is heading for a break-up?
faq.a: No. The matrix does not predict events or dates. The Tower in the middle of the tail describes how the couple lives its task: through rethinking what holds the home up. In the tale of Aladdin the palace comes back, and two people rule it.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Out of 3, 16 and 4 a couple's matrix forms only the order 3-16-4. The closest in meaning is 3-7-4: the same entry and the same main task, but with the Chariot in the middle.

faq.q: Who in the couple is Aladdin, and who is the princess?
faq.a: Either partner, and the roles change. The numbers speak about the couple, not about gender: the Chariot and the Hermit come from the partners' personal tails, but in real life both get to keep the lamp on the cornice and both get to swap it for a new one.

Now the princess wants the egg, and Aladdin at once finds the same flaw: whatever she lacks, he lacks too. The shared wish instantly becomes resistance, and the genie, with a cry, refuses to hang his own master under the dome. The last thing "for perfect completeness" can demand the very source of the couple's strength as its price.

Galland's ending: the sultan dies, the princess, "as lawful heir", takes the throne and shares the supreme power with Aladdin. "They reigned together for many years." In Andrew Lang's well-known English retelling what remains is "He succeeded the Sultan when he died, and reigned for many years." **The reteller did to the end of the tale what the Emperor at his worst does to a couple: one crown, one head.**

The strong version of the tail is Galland's ending. Every so often, list together what holds the home up, so that no lamp stands on a cornice only one partner knows about. When leaving, leave a map: where things are and what must not be changed without a call. Write the rules together and review them. After a collapse, the formula from Africa: one's own share of the blame, then straight to the plan. Before the last thing "for perfect completeness", ask whose wish it is. And the rule Scheherazade draws for a monarch: listen first, decide afterwards.
If threats, pressure or fear for each other appear in the home, this is no longer a task of the tail: a psychologist is needed then, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.meaning: Your task is to rule your home together: you both know what holds it up, and after a collapse you don't hunt for a culprit.
